cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Between two trees beside a stream, the haloed Christ stands holding a tall cross-staff and bends toward a small animal at the water's edge. The verse beneath reads 'virga tua et baculus tuus' — 'thy rod and thy staff they comfort me' — so that the Lord who is the shepherd of the psalm appears as Christ with the staff of the Cross.
facts: The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

Q18338551.summary: In a dense, turbulent nocturne, soldiers seize Christ while Judas presses close, and Peter, sword raised, attacks the servant Malchus in the foreground. Dürer's woodcuts brought the Passion to a broad public with an unprecedented range of tone and drama achieved through line alone.
facts: The Large Passion woodcuts were issued together as a book in 1511, with Latin verses by the Benedictine monk Benedictus Chelidonius; this sheet, dated 1510, is one of the later designs in the series.
Printed images allowed Dürer's compositions to circulate across Europe and beyond, where they were copied by other artists, including painters in Mughal India.
Dürer's prints were widely copied in his lifetime, and the 1511 book editions of his woodcuts warned off copyists by citing a privilege granted by Emperor Maximilian I.
